findings.issue_text: pkg/apiserver/rest/dualwriter_mode3.go:50 — [P1, confidence 100, blocking] Launching each mirror write with "go func() {" and returning before it completes removes ordering even between sequential acknowledged requests, so a create followed by a delete executes the legacy delete at line 112 before the delayed legacy create at line 55, leaving a resurrected legacy record after both requests succeed against unified storage with no queued reconciliation to restore consistency.

pkg/apiserver/rest/dualwriter_mode3.go:139 — [P1, confidence 75, blocking] Passing the original transformation through "_, _, errObjectSt := d.Legacy.Update(ctx, name, objInfo, createValidation, updateValidation, forceAllowCreate, options)" instead of wrapping the committed unified result re-evaluates partial updates against the legacy object, so when a prior mirror failure leaves an old playlist interval a title-only patch preserves that stale interval in legacy while unified storage retains its newer interval, permanently diverging the two APIs even though both update calls succeed.

pkg/apiserver/rest/dualwriter_mode3.go:51 — [P1, confidence 100, blocking] Deriving detached work from the request with `context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, time.Second*10, errors.New("legacy create timeout"))` cancels an unfinished legacy write when the successful HTTP request ends, so a slow legacy store loses acknowledged create/update/delete/delete-collection mirroring with no retry; the ten-second timeout does not extend the parent context's lifetime, and the same defect occurs at lines 110, 135, and 163.

pkg/apiserver/rest/dualwriter_mode3.go:106 — [P2, confidence 75, advisory] Recording `d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage)` places every successfully deleted resource name in the metric dimension otherwise populated by `options.Kind`, so sustained creation and deletion of distinct resources grows metric cardinality and exporter memory for operators; the strongest rebuttal is that this only enriches telemetry, but resource identity is unbounded and deleting the resource does not remove its metric series.

pkg/apiserver/rest/dualwriter_mode3.go:166 — [P2, confidence 100, advisory] Reporting a failed legacy collection deletion with `d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startLegacy)` attributes its sole failure signal to unified storage after the API has already reported success, while unified create/update failures are conversely recorded through `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage)` at lines 45 and 129, misleading operators during a backend outage; the strongest rebuttal is that best-effort mirror errors need not fail requests, but removing their error logs and labeling their only remaining signal as the healthy backend prevents accurate failure diagnosis.

pkg/apiserver/rest/dualwriter_mode3_test.go:53 — P1, confidence 100: `ls := legacyStoreMock{m, l}` and `us := storageMock{m, s}` share the same method expectations throughout the new suite and no test asserts separate backend calls or waits for replication, so routing Get/List to legacy or deleting every legacy-write goroutine still satisfies these unit tests and falsely certifies Mode3 routing and dual writes.

pkg/apiserver/rest/dualwriter_mode3_test.go:311 — P2 advisory, confidence 100: `m.On("Update", mock.Anything, input, mock.Anything, mock.Anything, mock.Anything, mock.Anything, mock.Anything).Return(exampleObj, false, nil)` returns a canned object without exercising UpdatedObjectInfo against either stored object, so the tests do not detect divergent patch results after removal of updateWrapper when legacy and unified old values differ; the strongest rebuttal is that playlist integration covers PATCH, but its ordinary CRUD sequence does not seed differing backend values or inspect callback execution against them.

pkg/apiserver/rest/dualwriter_mode3_test.go:65 — P2 advisory, confidence 100: `dw.Create(context.Background(), tt.input, func(context.Context, runtime.Object) error { return nil }, &metav1.CreateOptions{})` and the other new write tests use uncancellable contexts and immediately returning mocks without completion barriers, so they leave the new asynchronous request-cancellation and timeout lifecycle unverified for callers whose requests finish before legacy writes complete; the strongest rebuttal is that integration requests exercise real contexts, but none controls a blocked legacy operation and checks its outcome after request cancellation or its deadline.

pkg/apiserver/rest/dualwriter_mode3_test.go:68 — P2 advisory, confidence 100: `assert.Error(t, err)` is the only assertion in each new create/update failure case and the registry is never inspected anywhere in this suite, so existing tests accept unified-store failures recorded as legacy failures and legacy collection-delete durations recorded as storage durations, leaving operators with incorrectly attributed telemetry; the strongest rebuttal is that CRUD results are the unit-test contract, but this diff explicitly adds per-backend duration recording and its correctness cannot be observed through returned objects or errors.

adjudication_records.issue_text: pkg/apiserver/rest/dualwriter_mode3.go:50 — [P1, confidence 100, blocking] Launching each mirror write with "go func() {" and returning before it completes removes ordering even between sequential acknowledged requests, so a create followed by a delete executes the legacy delete at line 112 before the delayed legacy create at line 55, leaving a resurrected legacy record after both requests succeed against unified storage with no queued reconciliation to restore consistency.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows that in Mode3, legacy writes are now executed asynchronously via 'go func()' (lines 50-57 for Create, 108-115 for Delete, etc.) while the main function returns immediately after the unified storage operation completes. This means if a client sends a Create request followed by a Delete request, both unified storage operations complete in order, but the goroutines for legacy writes may execute out of order - the Delete goroutine could complete before the Create goroutine, leaving the legacy storage in an inconsistent state (record exists when it shouldn't). This is a real race condition introduced by the async pattern without any ordering guarantees.

adjudication_records.issue_text: pkg/apiserver/rest/dualwriter_mode3.go:139 — [P1, confidence 75, blocking] Passing the original transformation through "_, _, errObjectSt := d.Legacy.Update(ctx, name, objInfo, createValidation, updateValidation, forceAllowCreate, options)" instead of wrapping the committed unified result re-evaluates partial updates against the legacy object, so when a prior mirror failure leaves an old playlist interval a title-only patch preserves that stale interval in legacy while unified storage retains its newer interval, permanently diverging the two APIs even though both update calls succeed.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that in the Update method, the goroutine passes the original `objInfo` to Legacy.Update instead of wrapping the result from Storage.Update (the `res` object). In the old code, there was explicit wrapping: `d.Legacy.Update(ctx, name, &updateWrapper{upstream: objInfo, updated: obj}, ...)`. The new code just passes `objInfo` directly. This means the legacy store will re-evaluate the update against its own current state rather than applying the exact same object that was committed to unified storage. If the legacy store has stale data from a previous sync failure, this could cause divergence between the two stores.

adjudication_records.issue_text: pkg/apiserver/rest/dualwriter_mode3.go:51 — [P1, confidence 100, blocking] Deriving detached work from the request with `context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, time.Second*10, errors.New("legacy create timeout"))` cancels an unfinished legacy write when the successful HTTP request ends, so a slow legacy store loses acknowledged create/update/delete/delete-collection mirroring with no retry; the ten-second timeout does not extend the parent context's lifetime, and the same defect occurs at lines 110, 135, and 163.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies a real defect. Looking at line 51 in the diff: `ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, time.Second*10, errors.New("legacy create timeout"))` - this creates a child context from the request context `ctx`. When the goroutine runs asynchronously (via `go func()`), the parent request context will be cancelled when the HTTP request completes. Since `context.WithTimeoutCause` creates a child context, it will be cancelled when either: (1) the 10-second timeout expires, OR (2) the parent context is cancelled. If the HTTP response returns quickly (which it will since Storage.Create succeeded), the parent context cancels, killing the legacy write goroutine prematurely. The same pattern appears at lines 110, 135, and 163 for Delete, Update, and DeleteCollection respectively. This is a real correctness bug where legacy store mirroring can be silently dropped.

adjudication_records.issue_text: pkg/apiserver/rest/dualwriter_mode3_test.go:53 — P1, confidence 100: `ls := legacyStoreMock{m, l}` and `us := storageMock{m, s}` share the same method expectations throughout the new suite and no test asserts separate backend calls or waits for replication, so routing Get/List to legacy or deleting every legacy-write goroutine still satisfies these unit tests and falsely certifies Mode3 routing and dual writes.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that the test setup uses a shared mock (`m := &mock.Mock{}`) for both `legacyStoreMock` and `storageMock`. This means when tests set up expectations like `m.On("Get", ...)`, they don't distinguish which backend (legacy vs storage) receives the call. For Mode3, which should read from Storage and write to both, the tests don't verify that Legacy is NOT called for reads or that both backends receive writes. The goroutine-based legacy writes in the implementation (e.g., `go func() { d.Legacy.Create(...) }()`) are not awaited or verified in tests. However, this is a test quality/coverage concern rather than a bug in the implementation itself - the tests could pass even if routing logic were incorrect.
